What moves here is the body—in other words, matter.
His statement therefore means that matter cannot exist outside space, since it cannot move “in nothing,” and cannot exist outside time, since it cannot move “toward nothing.”
The second point follows from the fact that changes in material phenomena unfold through time, moving from the past to the present and then into the future.
Within the historical setting of his own period, al-Naẓẓām therefore arrives at a view containing the beginnings of a materialist and dialectical tendency.
First, matter cannot be separated from space and time.
Second, space and time cannot be separated from each other.
This early view fits closely with his materialist position on the endless division of material particles.

Every thing can interpenetrate with its opposite and with what differs from it. An opposite is something that resists and counteracts another thing, as sweetness opposes bitterness and heat opposes cold. Things that differ without being direct opposites include sweetness and coldness, or sourness and coldness.

He also held that something light may interpenetrate with something heavy. A light thing may have less volume than a heavy thing yet possess greater force. When it enters the heavy thing, it may occupy it.
In other words, something small in volume but great in force may occupy something large in volume but weak in force.
By “interpenetration” he meant that the space occupied by one body is also occupied by the other, so that one thing is inside the other.
We see a philosophical consistency with al-Naẓẓām’s two earlier ideas: his theory of motion and his theory of the endless division of material particles.
The connection becomes clearer once we place his remarks in their wider historical setting.
In speaking about the interpenetration of opposites, al-Naẓẓām brings us back to an old problem in the history of philosophy, one that goes back to the sixth and fifth centuries BCE.

This was the period in which a materialist tendency appeared among the Greek philosophers of Miletus and later in Heraclitus of Ephesus. At the same time, an idealist tendency began to emerge among the Pythagoreans and later among the Eleatics, especially Zeno of Elea.

As the materialist tendency developed and entered into conflict with idealist thought from the time of Pythagoras and the Pythagoreans onward, Heraclitus proposed that things are continually transformed into one another according to necessity.

He linked this to another idea: that opposites possess an inner unity and at the same time struggle against one another. This unity and struggle, in his view, are what drive the continual transformation of things.
Then, in the late fifth century BCE, Zeno of Elea denied the possibility of motion. His denial followed from his idealist and metaphysical outlook.
Zeno argued that both the existence of motion and even the attempt to think motion logically require contradiction. But he denied that contradiction can exist in nature.
His famous example of the flying arrow was meant to show why motion was impossible.

If an arrow is moving, Zeno argued, then at the same moment it must both be in a particular place and not be in that place. That is a contradiction. Since contradiction is impossible, motion itself must also be impossible.
To complete this background, we should note what the development of modern thought and science has shown.
Motion is not only an objective and universal reality in the world. It is also inseparable from contradiction understood as a real relationship between interpenetrating opposites.
Indeed, motion itself—which we accept as a real fact—cannot be understood without this contradiction.
In practice, contradiction means a relationship between two opposites that appears in the movement of things in three forms.
First, the two opposites possess an inner unity.
Second, they struggle against one another within that unity.
Third, the struggle is resolved through each side negating the other.
This negation is the real meaning of the transformation Heraclitus had already pointed toward in the sixth century BCE.
According to the dialectical law of their unity, struggle, and transformation, opposites therefore depend on one another and negate one another within a single connected process.

Throughout the history of philosophy, this question—the conflict of opposites—became one of the dividing lines between metaphysical and idealist thinkers on one side, and thinkers with materialist and dialectical tendencies on the other.

The first group denied that opposites and contradictions exist in nature at all, let alone that opposites can interpenetrate or form a unity. They reached this conclusion partly by treating nature in the same way they treated human statements, especially the statements of scholars and philosophers, where contradiction was something to be avoided.

The second group, by contrast, recognized all three features in the motion of matter: the inner unity of opposites, their struggle within that unity, and the eventual resolution of this struggle through their mutual negation.
With that background in mind, we can return to al-Naẓẓām’s statement that:
Every thing can interpenetrate with its opposite and with what differs from it,
Interpenetration means that the space occupied by one body is also occupied by the other, and that one of the two things is inside the other.
This fits closely with what he says elsewhere about motion as something universally present.

He affirms motion, and at the same time he says that one opposite can exist within another. He defines an opposite as something that “resists and counteracts” the other opposite or differing thing. He then defines interpenetration by saying that the two occupy the same space and that one is “inside” the other.
All of this strongly suggests that, in thinking through this problem, al-Naẓẓām again came close to the dialectical idea of both the inner unity and the conflict of opposites.
What else could it mean for two opposites to occupy the same space and for one to be inside the other, if not some form of inner unity?

And once this is accepted, what else could al-Naẓẓām mean by saying that each opposite “resists and counteracts” the other, if not a contradiction between them—a struggle taking place within their unity?

There may even be significance in al-Naẓẓām’s choice of the Arabic words translated here as “resists” and “counteracts.” Both are formed in a grammatical pattern that normally suggests reciprocal action between two sides.
That choice does not seem accidental or merely stylistic.

The reciprocal form implies motion, and it implies that the motion takes place within a single process involving two sides. Here that process is one of mutual resistance and counteraction—in other words, a struggle and contradiction between two sides occupying the same “space” and taking part in the same movement.

This is what we meant when we spoke of al-Naẓẓām’s consistency across two questions that, in the logic of reality and in dialectical thought, belong closely together: the question of motion and the question of the unity and contradiction of opposites.
A scientific researcher examining al-Naẓẓām’s treatment of these questions could hardly place him in the same camp as metaphysical and idealist thinkers.
This conclusion holds even if, for the moment, we limit ourselves to the three questions we have examined so far:
the division of material particles, motion in nature, and the interpenetration and struggle of opposites.

In our view, a thinker’s position on these three questions can tell us a great deal about the general character of his thought. They are central questions in determining where a thinker stands within the long philosophical conflict between materialism and idealism—a conflict that, directly or indirectly, is rooted in differences of ideological position.
But we must add an important scientific qualification.
Especially in an age such as al-Naẓẓām’s, it is extremely difficult to classify a thinker’s position on one question, or even several questions, in a final and absolute way.
Materialist and idealist elements, and metaphysical and dialectical elements, were often mixed together within the thought of the same person.

But this historical reality does not free the researcher from the task of identifying these different tendencies, showing the form each one takes in a particular thinker, and examining what it contains, while always keeping its historical setting in view.

Let us therefore continue examining al-Naẓẓām’s positions on some of the theoretical and intellectual questions disputed in his time. We may find further evidence confirming the intellectual and ideological character we have identified so far—or evidence that challenges it.
Al-Naẓẓām was reported to have said that length is the long thing itself and width is the wide thing itself.
He held that colors, tastes, smells, sounds, pains, heat, cold, moisture, and dryness are subtle bodies.
He held that the space occupied by a color may also be occupied by a taste and a smell, and that subtle bodies may exist together in a single space.
Several different ideas appear in this passage, but they all seem to come from the same starting point. We will return to that common starting point after looking at each idea separately.
First, al-Naẓẓām’s statement that “length is the long thing itself and width is the wide thing itself” resembles, in some respects, Aristotle’s view of essence.

For Aristotle, the essence of a thing arises from the thing’s own external existence. Essence therefore has no existence apart from the thing itself. In the external world, what actually exists is the thing, not a separate essence alongside it.
“Humanity,” for example, understood as a universal meaning or universal reality, does not possess an independent existence in the outside world. What actually exists is the individual human being.
This seems to be what al-Naẓẓām means when he says that length is the long thing and width is the wide thing.

Length and width do not exist independently in the external world as separate essences. What exists is the actual individual thing that is long or wide—the concrete example in which each quality appears.
The theoretical starting point of this view is opposition to the logic of Plato’s Forms.

In Platonism, the essence has an existence independent of the external thing. More than that, the external thing depends for its existence on the essence, or “Form,” so that the thing we encounter in the world is only an imperfect or shadow-like reflection of the true reality of the Form.
The Aristotelian starting point here clearly contains a materialist tendency. Its most important feature is that it recognizes the independent, objective existence of the external thing.
Al-Naẓẓām appears to accept the same starting point, in line with the tendency we have already seen in several of his other theories.
Second, al-Ashʿarī’s account tells us that al-Naẓẓām regarded smell, color, taste, sound, pain, heat, cold, moisture, and dryness not as purely abstract or immaterial things, but as material things.

In his view, they are “subtle bodies.” In other words, although they lack the visible density of ordinary bodies, they still possess the characteristics of things that exist materially in the objective world.
Modern science, of course, distinguishes between many of these phenomena and would not accept al-Naẓẓām’s single explanation for all of them.
But that is a separate issue.
We cannot expect a thinker who lived at such an early stage in the history of knowledge to have possessed the discoveries of our own age of extraordinary scientific development.
The important question here is the materialist starting point from which al-Naẓẓām tries to explain things.
For our present purpose, it matters less whether his explanation of one particular phenomenon was right or wrong. What matters is how he begins thinking about it, and where he begins from.

From this point of view, the account attributed to him by al-Ashʿarī again reveals a materialist tendency. Al-Naẓẓām assigns bodily characteristics even to something like pain, which in reality is a sensory response to something perceived through the senses.

Third, al-Naẓẓām’s claim that subtle bodies can exist together in the same space contains a dialectical element that is not very far removed from discoveries made by modern chemistry and physics about combinations in which natural properties and phenomena interpenetrate.
Fourth, the same passage gives us another confirmation of al-Naẓẓām’s view of motion as an absolute reality in the existence of matter.
D — Al-Ashʿarī also attributes the following view to al-Naẓẓām:
The spirit is a body, and it is the soul. The spirit is alive in itself.
He denied that life and power are meanings separate from the living and powerful being.

He held that the spirit exists in the body in such a way that the body is an affliction upon it and a cause that leads it to choose. If the spirit were freed from the body, its actions would take place by generation and necessity.
Elsewhere, al-Ashʿarī reports him as saying:
The human being is the spirit, but the spirit interpenetrates the body and is interwoven with it. All of this is in all of that, and all of that is in all of this. The body is an affliction upon it.
Al-Shahrastānī presents al-Naẓẓām’s view of the spirit, body, and human being somewhat differently:
He also followed the philosophers in saying that the human being, in the true sense, is the “soul” or “spirit,” while the body is its instrument and its mold.

But he did not fully grasp their doctrine and instead adopted the view of the natural philosophers among them. He said that the spirit is a subtle body interwoven with the physical body and penetrating every part of it, just as water is present in a rose, oil in sesame seeds, and butterfat in milk.
